title: A Giant Hidden Ocean Wave Is Raising Sea Levels on the West Coast
summary:
A huge wave you cannot see has been raising sea levels along the West Coast of the United States. It is called a Kelvin wave, and scientists say more are on the way.

A Kelvin wave is not a wall of water or a wave you could surf. "It's a planetary-scale wave," said Dillon Amaya, a scientist at North Carolina State University. It moves slowly beneath the ocean's surface and stretches for thousands of miles.

These waves can form along the equator during El Niño years, when a vast area of the Pacific Ocean becomes much warmer than usual. This year's strong El Niño sent warm water east under the sea until it reached South America. There, the wave split. Part of it traveled north along the West Coast, and part went south toward Chile. Columbia University professor Mark Cane compared it to "an enormous bathtub sloshing around."

As the wave moves up the coast, it gradually raises sea levels. Amaya said it does not cause floods by itself, but it makes flooding more likely when a big storm or very high tides arrive. In early October, sea levels in parts of Southern California were already about six to eight inches higher than normal. Then Tropical Storm Rachel brought a storm surge that flooded some neighborhoods.

Kelvin waves also carry warmer water, which can stress sea life. Tropical fish have shown up in unusual places, and a whale shark was spotted off San Diego.

The wave is named after Lord Kelvin, a British scientist who first described it in the late 1800s. Amaya expects the next Kelvin wave to reach San Diego in late October or early November, with several more through the fall and early winter.
why_it_matters: Higher sea levels can make storms more damaging for coastal neighborhoods, and warmer water can stress sea life, so understanding these waves helps communities prepare.

background_read: El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which ocean water in the tropical Pacific becomes much warmer than usual, which can shift weather around the world.
Warm water takes up a little more space than cold water, so when a large mass of it moves along a coast, the sea surface there rises slightly.
Coastal flooding usually happens when several things line up, such as high tides, strong storm winds pushing water ashore and an already higher sea level.
Scientists track these hidden ocean waves with measurements and computer models so coastal communities can prepare for higher flood risk.
